content: A tumbleweed is the above-ground portion of a plant that detaches from its roots once it has matured and dried. It is carried by the wind, rolling across the ground. In most cases, the tumbleweed consists of the entire plant except for the roots, but in some species, it is only the flower cluster. This phenomenon is most commonly observed in steppe and desert climates. The tumbleweed serves as a diaspore, facilitating the dispersal of seeds or spores. It achieves this by scattering its propagules either as it tumbles or after it comes to rest in a moist environment. In the latter scenario, the tumbleweed mechanically opens upon absorbing water, releasing its propagules, though the tumbleweed itself is no longer alive. The number of plant species that exhibit the tumbleweed habit is relatively small, but many of these species are common agricultural weeds. For example, several annual species of the genus Salsola (family Amaranthaceae), originally native to Eurasia, have become widespread in North America. These plants are so prevalent that they have become iconic symbols in Western films, often representing desolation in frontier landscapes. Salsola pestifera became naturalized across large areas of North America after being introduced from continental Asia, often as a contaminant in agricultural seed shipments. Similarly, Salsola kali is believed to have arrived in the United States in shipments of flax seeds to South Dakota during the 19th century. Another species, Salsola tragus (commonly known as Russian thistle), is an annual plant that detaches at the base of its stem, forming a tumbleweed that disperses its seeds as it rolls. This species was likely introduced to South Dakota from Russia in the 1870s through flaxseed shipments. It has since become a noxious weed, spreading throughout North America and thriving in disturbed soils such as roadsides, cultivated fields, and eroded slopes, as well as in natural habitats with sparse vegetation like coastal sands, riparian zones, semi-deserts, and deserts. Despite its status as a weed, Salsola tragus is sometimes used as forage for livestock in arid rangelands. Other members of the Amaranthaceae family that form tumbleweeds include Amaranthus albus, native to Central America but introduced and weedy in Europe, Asia, and Australia; Amaranthus graecizans, naturalized in North America from its native Africa; Amaranthus retroflexus; Corispermum hyssopifolium; Kochia; and Cycloloma atriplicifolium, also known as the plains tumbleweed. Atriplex rosea, commonly called the tumbling orach, is a member of the Chenopodiaceae family. In the Asteraceae family, Centaurea diffusa (a knapweed) forms tumbleweeds and is native to Eurasia but naturalized in much of North America. Another member of this family, Lessingia glandulifera, sometimes forms tumbleweeds and grows in desert areas, chaparral, and open pine forests of the western United States, typically on sandy soils. In the Fabaceae family, some species of the genus Psoralea and Baptisia tinctoria are reported to produce tumbleweeds. In the Plantaginaceae family, Plantago cretica forms tumbleweeds. In the Solanaceae family, Solanum rostratum exhibits this habit. In the Brassicaceae family, species such as Sisymbrium altissimum, Crambe maritima, Lepidium, and Anastatica (a resurrection plant) form tumbleweeds. Similar in habit to Anastatica but distantly related are the spore-bearing Selaginella lepidophylla (a lycopod) and members of the earthstar mushroom family (Geastraceae). These plants and fungi curl into a ball when dry and uncurl when moistened. Some species in the parsley family (Apiaceae) form tumbleweeds from their flower clusters (inflorescences). The garden plant baby's-breath (Gypsophila paniculata), in the pink family (Caryophyllaceae), has a dry inflorescence that forms tumbleweeds and has become a common weed in parts of central and western North America, including hayfields and pastures. In some species, the tumbleweed detaches from the plant through a process called abscission, where the plant stem separates. This has been observed in species like Psoralea and Kochia. Diaspores made of inflorescences also occur in some grasses, such as Schedonnardus paniculatus and certain species of Eragrostis and Aristida. In these plants, the inflorescences break off and tumble in the wind rather than the entire plant. Prominent examples of this adaptation include species of Spinifex from Southeast Asia, often referred to as tumble-grasses. In the United States, species like Panicum capillare and Eragrostis pectinacea are examples of tumble-grasses. In Southern Africa, genera of Amaryllidaceae such as Boophane, Crossyne, and to a lesser extent Brunsvigia, produce inflorescences in the form of globular umbels with long, spoke-like pedicels. These structures either remain at ground level or break off when the stems dry and the seeds ripen. These light, open, globular structures are highly effective tumbleweed diaspores, dispersing seeds within a few days as the follicles degrade during rolling. The seeds are fleshy, short-lived, and germinate rapidly where they land. Being poisonous and unpalatable, they are not attractive to animals for transport, making the rolling diaspore an effective dispersal strategy for these plants. Wind-dispersed fruits that tumble or roll on the ground, sometimes referred to as tumble fruits, are rare. Some of these are technically achenes. Highly inflated, indehiscent fruits that facilitate tumbling include genera such as Alyssopsis, Coluteocarpus, Physoptychis, and Physaria. Tumbleweeds have significant environmental effects, particularly on wind soil erosion in open regions. This is especially problematic in dry-land agricultural areas where additional moisture cannot be applied. For instance, a single Russian thistle plant can remove up to 44 gallons of water from the soil while competing with a wheat crop. The amount of water removed from fallow land, which is more prone to erosion, would be even higher. Beyond moisture consumption, the motion of tumbleweeds causes substantial damage to the protective soil crust, exposing the soil to further wind damage and topsoil loss. In visual media, tumbleweeds have become a powerful symbol, often associated with desolate, dry, and humorless locations with few or no inhabitants. They are frequently used in Western films to depict abandoned or bleak settings, with a tumbleweed rolling past accompanied by the sound of a dry, hollow wind. This imagery is sometimes employed in unexpected locations for comedic effect, such as in the opening credits of the film The Big Lebowski. Tumbleweeds are also used to punctuate awkward silences, such as after a bad joke or an absurd statement, with the plant rolling by in the background and the wind sound emphasizing the uncomfortable quiet, similar to the sound of crickets.
